tips.text: Formations are strongest when their flanks are protected.
High ground improves your ability to control an engagement.
Keep reserve troops behind the main line to respond to breakthroughs.
Cavalry is most effective when attacking exposed flanks or isolated units.
Avoid sending cavalry directly into prepared infantry formations.
Archers perform best when protected from direct melee combat.
Terrain can be as important as numbers. Use forests, hills, and narrow passages to your advantage.
A formation that becomes scattered is easier to surround and destroy.
Exhausted troops are less effective. Allow units time to recover when possible.
Protect your commander. Losing leadership at the wrong moment can decide a battle.
Direct commander control can help turn a critical fight, but exposes your commander to greater danger.
A well-defended position is one the enemy has not yet discovered a ridiculous way around.
Never underestimate the tactical value of looking busy while someone else carries the stone.
Cavalry can arrive quickly. Whether they should have arrived there is another question.
A commander who personally investigates every problem soon becomes one of them.
Walls are excellent defenses until someone remembers gates exist.
If your formation looks impressive from a distance, you are at least halfway to military competence.
The enemy cannot predict your strategy if you have forgotten it yourself.
Every supply shortage begins with someone saying, “We probably have enough.”
War elephants are powerful, disciplined weapons of war, right up until they have an opinion.
History remembers the victorious general. The quartermaster remembers who forgot to bring food.
Use patrol orders to secure roads, settlements, and vulnerable resource routes.
Workers are valuable strategic assets. Do not leave them exposed near the front.
Stockpiles shorten resource delivery routes and improve economic efficiency.
Building near resources can reduce the amount of time workers spend carrying supplies.
A strong economy cannot help you if the enemy cuts the road between it and your army.
Repairing damaged defenses before the next attack is usually cheaper than rebuilding them afterward.
Capturing useful infrastructure can be more valuable than destroying it.
Watch your supply routes when advancing deep into hostile territory.
War elephants can disrupt formations, but unsupported elephants can quickly become isolated.
Wildlife may react unpredictably to nearby troops and fighting.
Wolves are considerably less impressed by military rank than your soldiers are.
Scout unfamiliar terrain before committing your main force.
Keep an escape route available when fighting near rivers, cliffs, or narrow passages.
A retreat made early can preserve an army. A retreat made late can become a rout.
Concentrating your forces can overwhelm a stronger enemy fighting in separate groups.
Do not chase fleeing enemies so far that your own formation collapses.
An army marches on its stomach. The stomach, regrettably, also requires a supply line.
Enemy reinforcements are much less dangerous when they never reach the battlefield.
Every commander has a plan until a sheep joins the formation.
Destroying an enemy army is useful. Preventing it from fighting effectively is often enough.
Infantry can hold ground that faster units may struggle to defend.
Keep ranged troops away from routes enemy cavalry can reach quickly.
Battles are often decided before contact through positioning, preparation, and logistics.
A narrow front can prevent a numerically superior enemy from using all of its troops at once.
When defending, force the enemy to come to you under unfavorable conditions.
When attacking, look for weak points rather than spreading damage evenly across the enemy line.
A unit surrounded on several sides will struggle even if it began the fight at full strength.
The Iron Sepulcher is best approached with troops prepared for an unexpected engagement.
A grave priest mends the dead around it and hurls fire at the living. Strike it down before the line closes.
Skeleton guardians defend their ruins and drift back to them when the fight moves on. Draw them out, or bring the fight to the stones.
A cursed shrine cannot be attacked while its guardians stand. Break the guard, then purify the shrine by capturing it.
Ranged troops and a Medicus make the vigil survivable. Wound the dead from a distance, and keep the wounded living.
The dead do not tire, do not flee, and do not file complaints. They are, in every other respect, a poor garrison.
Clearing a dangerous area is not the same as securing it. Check what remains nearby.
The shortest path between two points is rarely the route selected by an army.
Hannibal Barca was the Carthaginian commander who brought the Second Punic War into Italy by marching across the Alps in 218 BC.
Hannibal married a woman from the Iberian city of Castulo. The poet Silius Italicus calls her Imilce; the historian Livy does not give her name.
Hamilcar Barca, Hannibal's father, built Carthaginian power in Iberia after the First Punic War. His sons inherited a formidable campaign.
In 218 BC Hannibal crossed the Alps with infantry, cavalry, baggage, and elephants. His exact route remains disputed.
At the Trebia, Hannibal lured Roman troops into a winter battle; a concealed Carthaginian force struck during the fighting.
At Lake Trasimene in 217 BC, Hannibal ambushed a Roman marching column between the lake and the hills. Terrain was part of the trap.
At Cannae in 216 BC, Hannibal's yielding center drew Roman infantry forward while his flanks and cavalry closed around them.
Maharbal commanded cavalry under Hannibal. The famous tale that he urged an immediate march on Rome after Cannae comes from later Roman tradition.
Hasdrubal Barca was Hannibal's brother, not his brother-in-law Hasdrubal the Fair. His attempted reinforcement ended at the Metaurus in 207 BC.
Fabius Maximus earned the name 'the Delayer' by avoiding Hannibal's preferred pitched battles and harassing his movements and supplies.
Scipio took New Carthage in 209 BC, seizing an important harbor, stores, and hostages instead of chasing every enemy army.
At Ilipa in 206 BC, Scipio changed his usual deployment and attacked the Carthaginian wings with his stronger Roman infantry.
At Zama in 202 BC, Scipio left lanes through his infantry to blunt Hannibal's elephants. Positioning beat panic.
Masinissa's Numidian horsemen fought alongside Rome at Zama. Their return to the battlefield helped decide the fight.
Hannibal won battles in Italy, but Rome's alliances, manpower, and stubborn refusal to surrender kept the war alive.
Hannibal's elephants crossed mountains. Your supply wagon still insists that a shallow stream is impassable.
A brilliant encirclement is harder to admire from the inside.
Fabius called it patience. His critics probably called it a very long walk.
The cavalry has found the enemy's rear. Unfortunately, it has also found your missing supplies.
A battle plan with seven arrows usually requires at least eight messengers.
The best time to discover that your bridge is too narrow was before the elephants arrived.
A general can order a forced march. Boots remain stubbornly outside the chain of command.
The Iron Sepulcher keeps no quartermaster. Its garrison stopped asking for rations centuries ago.
Sepulcher legend says grave priests draw their fire from the last breaths trapped beneath the iron seals of forgotten shrines.
Some say a grave priest burns the names scraped from burial stones. Each lost name feeds one more ember.
The Sepulcher's iron nails are said to pin unfinished oaths beneath the earth. Its guardians are still keeping theirs.
Soldiers whisper that the shrine's haze repeats orders in the voices of men who never came home.
A grave priest appears to mend broken bone. The darker story is that it persuades the grave to return what it claimed.
The Sepulcher's guardians do not pursue forever. They return to the shrine as though the last watch never ended.
An undead shrine is warded while its guardians live. Defeat every wave before attempting to destroy or capture it.
Slaying the last guardian clears a zone, but the shrine is not purified until you capture or destroy it.
No one remembers who buried the first Sepulcher priest. The priest has had plenty of time to hold a grudge.
A grave priest never runs short of fire. It only asks whose name is missing from the graveyard roll.
The dead have held this post for centuries. You can understand why they dislike a change of ownership.
